The ground, already near saturation, has a limited capacity to absorb this rainfall. What: Additional rainfall amounts of 20 mm. Locally higher amounts possible. When: Today through Thursday. Additional information: A few more rounds of showers and embedded thunderstorms are possible through Thursday. Portions of the region have received significant rainfall amounts over the last few days. As a result, any further rainfall could have significant impacts. Rainfall warnings may be issued for some regions. Rainfall amounts will likely be highly variable across the region. Water will likely pool on roads and in low-lying areas. Toronto Star Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Print Copy article link Save The Artemis II crew’s wakeup playlist. Spotify screen capture Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Print Copy article link Save Home News Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email The Artemis II crew is heading back to Earth, with splashdown scheduled for Friday, April 10, 2026. NASA photo Facebook Twitter WhatsApp LinkedIn SMS Email Print Copy article link Save After a 10-day mission around the moon, the Artemis II mission is coming to an end with a scheduled splashdown on Friday.As Artemis II nears its return to Earth, NASA teams are on the ground preparing for Orion’s re-entry and splashdown in the Pacific Ocean off the coast of San Diego, Calif. Already a Subscriber? Sign in You are logged in Switch accounts Secure transaction. Cancel anytime. When is Artemis II’s splashdown time? ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW Powered By 10 What's your desert island movie?ShareNextStay Splashdown is scheduled for around 8:07 p.m. (local time in southern Ontario) on Friday, April 10, off the coast of San Diego, Calif.“As Orion descends through about 400,000 feet, the spacecraft will enter a planned six‑minute communications blackout as plasma forms around the capsule during peak heating,” according to NASA. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW During peak heating, the capsule’s heat shield will experience temperatures of around 2,760 C — about twice as hot as molten lava.Inside, the crew is expected to experience up to 3.9 Gs in a typical landing. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW Within two hours after splashdown, NASA says the crew will be extracted from Orion and flown to the USS John P. Murtha. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW “Recovery teams will retrieve the crew using helicopters, and once aboard the ship, the astronauts will undergo post‑mission medical evaluations before returning to shore to board an aircraft bound for NASA’s Johnson Space Center in Houston,” NASA explained.How to watch the Artemis II missionNASA has provided live coverage of prelaunch, launch and mission events, and will conclude with the coming splashdown.NASA live coverageBriefings, events and 24-7 mission coverage will be on NASA’s YouTube channel, and events will each have their own stream closer to their start time.You can watch the live return coverage on NASA+, Amazon Prime, Apple TV, Netflix, HBO Max, Discovery+, Peacock and Roku starting at 6:30 p.m. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW Coverage will continue until NASA and Department of Defense personnel safely assist the crew out of Orion and transport them to the USS Murtha.NASA content is available through a variety of online platforms, including social media.Canadian Space AgencyThe Canadian Space Agency will host a bilingual event at the John H. Chapman Space Centre in Longueuil, Que., for splashdown.Three space-to-Earth connections will be livestreamed on the CSA’s Facebook page and YouTube channel.Who are the astronauts? ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW NASA astronauts Reid Wiseman, Victor Glover and Christina Koch, along with Canadian Space Agency (CSA) astronaut Jeremy Hansen, are on a 10-day journey around the moon aboard the Orion spacecraft.By the end of the mission, the crew will have travelled 2 million kilometres. When they reached the furthest point of the mission, 406,773 kilometres away from Earth, the crew surpassed the record for human spaceflight’s farthest distance previously set by Apollo 13.Artemis II is the first time humans have gone to the moon in over 50 years, since Apollo 17.“For Canada, this mission started with a bold vision and a deep-rooted faith in Canadian know-how. Today, we can proudly say that our country is helping write a page of space exploration history,” said Hansen from space in a conversation with Prime Minister Mark Carney on April 8. News It’s made in Ontario and just made history in space. Nutella’s viral moment on Artemis II moon livestream Janis Ramsay Artemis II Wakeup Songs Spotify Playlist ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW Even astronauts need to pump up the jams to wake up.NASA has released the official wake-up song playlist for the Artemis II mission on Spotify, featuring songs selected by the crew for their historic 10-day journey around the moon.The crew has chosen a mix of songs, including the popular classic hit “Under Pressure,” a Queen and David Bowie’s collab, and the new pop cult classic “Pink Pony Club” by Chappell Roan. The Artemis II crew’s wakeup playlist. Spotify screen capture The Space Launch System rocket took off from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida on Wednesday, April 1.Artemis II is now on its way back to Earth after the historic flyby of the moon. Splashdown is scheduled for Friday, April 10, which will occur off the coast of San Diego, Calif. Canadian connections ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW Jenni Gibbons, 37, of Calgary, is the first Canadian to serve in the ground control role of capsule communicator, or capcom, for the Artemis II mission.“This is a really critical role. She’s the primary point of contact between the crew and mission control,” said Rachel Ward-Maxwell, researcher-programmer of astronomy and space sciences at the Ontario Science Centre. Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jenni Gibbons explains her role as a capsule communicator, or capcom, for the Artemis II mission. Who is Jeremy Hansen?Hansen was born in London, Ont., and raised on a farm in nearby Ailsa Craig.His journey into aviation and to the moon began in 1988 at age 12, when he joined the 614 Royal Canadian Air Cadet Squadron, according to the Government of Canada.After earning a private pilot’s licence, a bachelor’s degree in space science, serving a term as a fighter pilot and graduating from Astronaut Candidate Training, he became the first Canadian entrusted with leading a NASA astronaut class. ARTICLE CONTINUES BELOW “For as long as I can remember, I was fascinated by space exploration,” Hansen said in a video posted to the government’s website.“I looked at a photograph of Neil Armstrong standing on the moon, and I wanted to see what it would be like to leave this planet and look at it from beyond.”In 2023, he was assigned to the Artemis II mission, and is now about to make history.“I’m thrilled to be part of the next generation of space explorers to the moon as I join the historic Artemis II mission, the first crewed mission to leave lower orbit since 1972,” he said before the mission.“I can’t wait to see our planet from afar as backdrop to the moon.” Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen will be the first Canadian to orbit the moon as part of the Artemis II crew. Toronto Star What is the goal of the Artemis II mission?This mission is a crewed flight and a stepping-stone for future exploration on the moon. It follows the uncrewed Artemis I mission in 2022.Ward-Maxwell said the mission will allow the crew to test various systems and even identify possible landing sites on the moon. During the flyby of the moon, Artemis II took photos of the moon’s surface. In this image provided by NASA, the Artemis II crew captured this image of the Vavilov Crater on the Moon during a lunar flyby, Monday. NASA “It is really a stepping-stone to the moon and the eventual sustained presence on the moon,” she said.The Artemis II astronauts are expected to surpass the record for human’s farthest distance from Earth (400,171 kilometres), which was set by Apollo 13.The four-astronaut crew, launched using the Space Launch System, one of the world’s most powerful rockets, are travelling in what the Ontario Science Centre described as “a camper-van sized capsule” called the Orion spacecraft. Canadian Space Agency astronaut Jeremy Hansen, the first Canadian to fly around the moon, expresses his heartfelt thanks to all Canadians whose dedication, expertise and support made Canada’s participation in the historic Artemis II mission possible.
